This is part one of a two part post highlighting *Napistu*; a new framework for building genome-scale networks of molecular biology and biochemistry and interrogating them with high-dimensional data.

In this post, we will set the stage by discussing a common real-world use case - identifying the common regulators and characteristic pathways of a set of genes. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) is the bioinformatics warhorse for tackling this problem, but its limited by up-front definitions of gene sets, and is challenged when we are working with multiple data types. By mapping transcripts, proteins, metabolites, drugs, etc. onto entities in a graph we can transcend these limitations. But, in doing so, we'll strive to maintain the ease-of-use of GSEA.



The goal of this is to generate a set of molecular profiles, each of which contains a summary statistic for a large number of features from one or more data modalities.

In the following post, we will discuss how we can connect each profile to a network graph and apply network propagation to let information flow from the symptoms of a disease to its upstream regulatory causes.


In this series, I'll also reflect on the mechanics of performing these types of analyses in the era of genAI and AI-assisted coding. Many of us are trying to find the sweet spot between unaugmented software development and vibe coding. I'll call out the AI tools and workflows that I used and what they did well versus where they failed spectacularly.

## Strategy for creating profiles

1. EDA (explore the major drivers of variation)
   a. what are the relevant measures of disease severity?
   b. are there batch effects?
   c. what statistical models should we use to identify features
2. Supervised analysis
   a. regression
3. Unsupervised analysis
   a. multivariate factor analysis


This seems like a pretty good playbook for capturing the disease’s biology. The problem though is that I normally perform EDA and statistical analysis in R. But, I wanted to stick with Python for this work because Napistu is a Python framework and I wanted to build up support for funneling these types of datasets' findings into it.

To address this, I wanted to develop and utilize a codebase which satisfied several constraints
- performs the key analyses supporting each problem
- scientifically accurate
- developable in little time

This seems to be a classic case of the eternal software problem, you can't have all of {fast, good, and cheap}, pick two. Can genAI help us to achieve all three? It's very good at fast & cheap so we can use them to create good analyses.

- Brittle - tries to get too fancy by building advanced features; many arguments; no testing
- Unmaintainable - writing mountains of code; little focus on refactoring; limited docstrings; no type hints
Wrong - brittle and unmaintainable code is not the end of the world in a 1-off analysis but genAI can make implementation decisions which are scientifically inaccurate. A couple that I ran into during this analysis are:
Parsing the dependent variables out a regression formula (e.g., y ~ a + b) and turning it into separate tests (y ~ a & y ~ b).
- Treating p-values and q-values interchangeably where if q-values are missing it would filter on p-values < fdr_cutoff to identify discoveries.

The scary part is that wrong details can be hidden under layers of brittle, unmaintainable code.
